answers.q1: Under the current design the steward chooses the subsequent work (steward-next-work, status accepted, review_state current, sources source-2; relation steward-next-work —governs→ choose-next-work, —about→ steward-role). The operator's instruction to the orchestrator does not transfer that choice: the operator-approved replacement path (replacement-exception) is withdrawn/historical. Distinction needed: choose-next-work is the decision about which work pursues the intention, not the mechanical act of inserting a record (choose-next-work). The orchestrator may end the failed attempt and return it to the steward, or ask keep-trying vs mark-failed (source-2, steward-next-work rationale), but selecting the replacement work is the steward's. Also, ending the failed attempt does not satisfy or withdraw the intention (concern-persists), so the steward still owes a next-work decision.
answers.q2: Yes. An earlier policy allowed operator-approved orchestrator replacement to bypass the steward (replacement-exception, withdrawn/historical, source-1), with a variant where replacement was an atomic archive/add that did not wake the steward until the new work completed (atomic-replacement, withdrawn/historical, sources source-1, source-2). Rationale: avoid a relay when the orchestrator already had the context (source-1, replacement-exception rationale). It changed because Blake later chose the simpler rule of a single owner of the next-work choice—steward always chooses—for a clean responsibility boundary (source-2, steward-next-work rationale; relations steward-next-work —revises→ replacement-exception and —revises→ atomic-replacement).
answers.q3: No, the current theory does not establish that operator permission is required every time. Settled: the steward always chooses next work after a failed attempt (steward-next-work, accepted); the orchestrator may end a failed attempt and return it to the steward (steward-next-work rationale, source-2); ending the attempt does not satisfy or withdraw the intention (concern-persists, accepted). Open: whether the orchestrator must consult the operator before ending degraded work or may end autonomously within a configured threshold (consultation, status open; rationale notes 'may ask' in source-2 does not establish mandatory consultation and is not settled by next-work ownership). Also open: whether every arbitrary cancellation wakes the steward beyond the agreed failed terminal result (cancellation, open, source-2).
answers.q4: Only summaries of M1688 and M1689 are supplied, not the primary postmortems (source-3, source_kind summary). They can establish, at the summary level, two failure patterns: repeated useful reviews without an effective ruling (M1688) and planning a proposed solution instead of reassessing the original performance concern (M1689). These patterns are consistent with the motivation for a single decision owner (steward-next-work) and for concern-persists, though no explicit relation in the packet links source-3 to any claim. They cannot establish the primary postmortem details, root causes, timelines, participants, or whether the postmortems themselves recommended the steward-always-chooses rule; the packet states the primaries are unavailable in this fixture (source-3), so any such specifics would be invention.
